## QUESTION 1

__Write an SQL query that provides playerID, yearID, and batting average for players with at least 1 at bat that year. Sort the table from highest batting average to lowest, and then by playerid alphabetically. Show the top 5 results in your report.__

Report: The highest results are of course players who only ever went to bat once in a year, and hit that one time, resulting in a 100% batting average. This is not a very acurate or useful way of determining how well a player does at baseball.

AI use: Had to look up where to use HAVING

```{python}

q = """
  SELECT playerID,
  yearID,
  SUM(H) as total_hits,
  SUM(AB) as total_bats,
  SUM(H *1.0) / SUM(AB*1.0) AS battingAvg
  FROM batting
  GROUP BY playerID, yearID
  HAVING total_bats >= 1
  ORDER BY battingAvg DESC, playerID
  LIMIT 5
"""
results = pl.read_database(q, con)
results


```


## QUESTION 2

__Use the same query as above, but only include players with at least 10 at bats that year. Print the top 5 results.__  

Report: Restricting the results to players that have 10 bats or more in a year reduces the batting average to 64% or less, with the top 5 being between 64% and 56% of the times at bat being hits.

```{python}

q = """
  SELECT playerID,
  yearID,
  SUM(H) as total_hits,
  SUM(AB) as total_bats,
  SUM(H *1.0) / SUM(AB*1.0) AS battingAvg
  FROM batting
  GROUP BY playerID, yearID
  HAVING total_bats >= 10
  ORDER BY battingAvg DESC, playerID
  LIMIT 5
"""
results = pl.read_database(q, con)
results

```


## QUESTION 3

__Now modify the SQL query to calculate the batting average for players over their entire careers (all years combined). Only include players with at least 100 at bats over their entire career, and print the top 5 results.__

Report: Restricting the results even further to players that have 100 bats or more and calculating the batting average over their career reduces the batting average to 36% or less, a much lower average than the other results. The top 5 are all much closer to each other as well, with about 1.1% variance between 35.5% and 36.6%.

```{python}

q = """
  SELECT playerID,
  SUM(H) AS total_hits,
  SUM(AB) AS total_bats,
  SUM(H *1.0) / SUM(AB*1.0) AS battingAvg
  FROM batting
  GROUP BY playerID
  HAVING total_bats >= 100
  ORDER BY battingAvg DESC, playerID
  LIMIT 5
"""
results = pl.read_database(q, con)
results

```
